cells.tense: Fairness is running through how you feel alongside people right now, and the pen stays steady in your hand.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Sit with one bond that has run its course, name to yourself what it was for, and give what is still alive in it your attention instead.
cells.core:
You feel alongside people, and the feeling moves fairly. You can sit where something hard is happening and stay level, which is not numbness — you are in it, and the temperature is right. People bring you the thing half-spoken and leave with something clearer. That is why what happens between you tends to settle instead of stick.
One bond has run its course, and keeping it held open costs more than it used to. Clearing it is not a cruelty. Sit with it once, name what it was for, and that it's done — then let what is actually alive in it have some space. What remains gets honest, and what was good about it keeps its shape.
cells.sheetLine: You feel with people fairly, and the field settles around you.
cells.verb: governing the emotional field of a room with fair judgment
cells.place: in the alignment between you and the people around you

cells.tense: You are already living through next month's argument in your head, and the fairness in you has become a ledger nobody asked to keep.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: For a week, each time you catch yourself pre-running a conversation, stop and steady one thing that is squarely here — one act, nothing past it.
cells.core:
You arrive before the event does. Next week's gathering already played out in your head, parts assigned, the scale out. Upcoming exchanges get balanced in advance, and the people who show up find they were already settled somewhere they didn't know about. The fairness is doing work nobody can feel yet, and from the far side it can look like control.
Set the whole weight down and put one turn of it where it can actually bear. Steady hands hold heavy stone by staying with the course they're on. Do one thing that's here and solid — one turn, everything down. What you were bracing for probably shifts shape by the time it lands, and the fixing can wait for the moment that needs it.
cells.sheetLine: You are balancing a conversation that hasn't happened yet.

cells.tense: For a while now you have been standing near the doorway of a place you left some time back.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Set down what happened in one recent exchange — the events in the order they came, nothing about how any of it felt.
cells.core:
You used to be easy in a group — feeling what they felt and knowing where it was going. Lately you watch from the edge. Somebody comes close and something in you stays put, and the connection runs on one side, and you are not sure where your own relation to either of them went. You are here and not here, and you can feel the difference yourself.
Take a recent exchange and set the events down as they occurred — what was said, what came next — with nothing about how it felt. The sequence will arrange itself the way a record does, and one moment will be the point where you stepped back. Look at that point without judging it. If what you see is that you have been doing this since some specific day, you can decide from a set of facts instead of a fog. The feeling can come later, or not.
cells.sheetLine: You watch from the edge of what you used to enter.

cells.tense: Something in how you read a room is already working, and you keep calling it luck when it isn't.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Try this for a month: when you understand something about a person before they say it, notice how you got it, then act or don't.
cells.core:
You read rooms well — who is about to move, which way a mood is tipping — and your account of it is that you just have a feeling. The person who got it right and the person describing it are using different words. What you have is not mood, exactly; it holds up when you check it later, and the story skips the one who saw it.
Pause after the next of those reads, before you do anything about it. Look at what you got and ask how it came to you — the pause, the missed word, the shift in the air. It holds when it is looked at honestly. It falls when you dress it up or write it off too quickly. Then act on it or don't. Either way you were there for it, which is the whole difference between a gut feeling and sight.
cells.sheetLine: You keep calling it a feeling. It keeps being true.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person actually governs anyone's feelings, decides anything, or holds authority anywhere — that is the archetype's flavor, not a fact about them. A reader could fairly say 'I don't govern anything, I just feel what a room feels,' and the Too Much and Too Little cells lean hardest on that unsupported claim, so their asks stay useful even if the read is wrong: counting your own share and writing plain facts both work for someone who never had authority. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you decide for the room' — cut.
